transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I’m here because I feel like I’m the only one actually looking closely at what happened around my father’s death. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records make sense, and the donation emails all line up, and that I’m reading too much into it, but when I compare the timestamps and the missing attachments and then the way certain people in the community avoid answering simple questions, it’s… I mean, it’s obvious to me someone is hiding something.

I’m a computer systems analyst, so I’m not just guessing. I notice patterns, I know when records don’t line up cleanly, and there are these gaps that people keep brushing off as “normal” or “administrative mistakes.” But they don’t feel normal. Not when the same people get quiet or change the subject when I ask about specific times or emails. I came in because my family thinks I should talk to someone, but honestly, I want someone to actually listen and not just tell me to drop it.
Do you believe that others are involved in a plot or conspiracy regarding your father's death?

Yes. I mean, I wouldn’t use the word “plot” lightly, because I know how that sounds, but… yes, I think other people are involved in keeping something hidden.

Everyone keeps saying the hospital records make sense, and the donation emails line up, and that I’m just connecting unrelated things. But when I actually compare the timestamps and look at the missing attachments, and then I ask certain people in the community straightforward questions and they dodge them or suddenly get vague, it’s hard to believe that’s all coincidence.

I’m not saying I know every single person’s role, or that I have the whole picture laid out perfectly, but it feels obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. And the more people tell me to stop looking, the more it feels like they don’t want me to find it.
Do you often find yourself questioning the intentions of people in your daily life, outside of the situation with your father's death?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I don’t think I go around assuming everyone has bad intentions, if that’s what you mean. Like, at work I can be cautious, sure, but that’s also just part of my job—if something doesn’t line up, I check it. I don’t think that’s the same as mistrusting people.

Outside of my father’s situation, I guess I do notice inconsistencies sometimes, but I don’t know that I’d say I’m questioning people’s intentions all the time. This feels different. This isn’t like thinking the cashier was rude on purpose or a coworker is trying to undermine me. This is about specific records, specific emails, specific people avoiding specific questions. So… no, not in some broad everyday way, at least not that I’ve noticed.
Do you find yourself questioning the intentions of your close friends or family members in situations unrelated to your father's death?

I don’t think so… not in situations that have nothing to do with my father, no. I mean, with family it’s complicated because lately almost every conversation somehow circles back to that, even if it starts out being about dinner or work or something ordinary. So it’s hard to separate cleanly.

But if you mean, like, do I think my sister is secretly working against me when we’re talking about normal family stuff, or do I think a close friend has some hidden motive if they cancel plans—no, not really. I might wonder if people are avoiding certain topics because they’re uncomfortable, but I don’t think I generally sit there analyzing everyone’s motives all the time.

I do pay attention to tone and timing and whether someone gives a straight answer, but that’s just… I don’t know, that’s how I am. And given everything, it feels reasonable to be alert. But unrelated to my father’s death specifically? I haven’t really noticed myself distrusting close friends or family in that broader way.
How long have you been thinking that someone is hiding something about your father's death?

About nine months, I think. It started after my father died, when I was going through his things—his records, messages, emails, that sort of thing. At first it wasn’t like I woke up one day and thought, “Someone is hiding something.” It was more gradual than that.

I was trying to organize everything, make sense of paperwork, accounts, messages people had sent, and I kept running into things that didn’t quite fit. So I’d tell myself, okay, maybe I’m tired, maybe I’m grieving, maybe I’m reading too much into it. But then another thing would come up, and another, and the feeling just… stayed.

So if you’re asking how long I’ve had this concern in a real way, not just a passing thought, I’d say roughly nine months—basically since that period after his death when I started sorting through his records and messages.
Have you ever ended a friendship or relationship because you believed the other person couldn't be trusted?

I haven’t really ended a friendship outright over it, no. Not like I sat someone down and said, “I don’t trust you, we’re done.” It’s been more… strained, I guess.

My work has mostly stayed steady, which I think is important to say because I’m not falling apart or anything. I still do my job, I still meet deadlines, I still handle systems issues and follow through on things. But with family, there’s definitely been a shift. Some relatives have started avoiding conversations with me, or they keep things very short, because they know I might bring up the records or the emails or what I think was concealed.

And I can tell when they’re steering around it. They’ll change the subject quickly, or say they have to go, or make it about me “needing to move on,” which is frustrating because I’m not trying to ruin every conversation. I just want straight answers. So no, I don’t think I’ve ended a relationship because of trust exactly, but some relationships have become more distant because they don’t want to talk about it.
Do you often find yourself wondering if people are telling you the truth in everyday conversations?

Not often, no—at least I don’t think so in ordinary conversations. If someone at work tells me they finished something, or a friend says they’re running late, I’m not usually sitting there thinking, “Are they lying to me?” I can take normal things at face value.

I do sometimes notice little hesitations or changes in wording, but I think a lot of people do that, especially if the topic is uncomfortable. So I might wonder for a second what they mean, but it doesn’t usually become this big thing unless the conversation is connected to my father or to things people have already been evasive about.

So… everyday conversations, no, not really. I wouldn’t say I’m constantly questioning everyone. It’s more specific than that.
Do you feel like you're questioning people's honesty or motives in situations that have nothing to do with your father's death or your work as a computer systems analyst?

No, I don’t think it really spills over into unrelated situations. I mean, I’m not walking around assuming the cashier has some hidden agenda or that coworkers are secretly plotting something. It’s not like that.

What I keep coming back to is my father’s death. That’s where the questions are. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records make sense, that the donation emails line up, that I’m just seeing gaps because I’m looking too closely. But when I actually compare things—the timestamps, the attachments that are missing, the way certain people in the community suddenly avoid answering basic questions—it does not look normal to me.

And I know that probably sounds like I’m being suspicious in general, but to me it’s specific. If someone lies about lunch plans, I don’t care. If someone changes the subject when I ask why an email about my father’s donations has a timestamp that doesn’t match the record they sent me, that’s different. That’s not random mistrust. That’s someone hiding something, or at least acting like they are. So outside of that whole situation, no, I don’t think I’m questioning people’s motives much. But around my father’s death, yes, absolutely.
Do you generally assume that people will take advantage of you if they can?

No, I wouldn’t say I generally assume that. I don’t go into every interaction thinking someone is looking for a way to use me or get something over on me.

I mean, people can be self-interested, sure. At work especially, you learn that people may avoid blame or frame things in a way that makes them look better. But that’s different from assuming they’ll take advantage of me if they can. Most of the time I deal with people pretty normally. If someone asks for help, I don’t automatically think there’s a hidden trap in it.

I guess I’m careful in certain situations, but I don’t think of myself as someone who believes everyone is out to exploit me. That feels too broad. I’d need a reason to think that about a person.
Do you often feel like you're being watched or followed, even when you're alone or in public places?

No, not really. I mean, I notice people around me the way anyone would—like if someone is walking behind me on the sidewalk for a few blocks, I might be aware of it, but I don’t usually think they’re following me.

And when I’m alone, I don’t have this feeling like someone is watching through the window or tracking me or anything like that. In public places, I’m more likely to be thinking about where I’m going or whatever I need to get done. I might look around if a place feels crowded or if someone is acting strange, but that’s more just normal awareness, I think.

So no, I wouldn’t say that’s something I often feel.
Do you think most people would lie to you if it suited their purposes?

I don’t think I’d put it that broadly, no. “Most people” feels like too sweeping of a statement to me. I know people lie sometimes if it helps them avoid embarrassment or consequences, or if they think the truth is inconvenient. I’m not naïve about that. But I don’t walk around assuming that most people are just waiting for the right opportunity to lie to me.

I usually judge it by the situation. If someone has a clear reason to hide something, or if what they’re saying doesn’t match the facts, then yes, I’m going to question it. But if it’s just ordinary day-to-day interactions, I don’t automatically assume dishonesty. That would be exhausting, honestly.

So I guess my answer is no—not as a general rule. I think some people would lie if it suited them, but I don’t assume most people would.
Do you think your suspicions about people hiding things from you are mostly about your father's death, or do you find yourself having similar suspicions in other areas of your life?

It’s mostly about my father’s death. I don’t think I’m walking around applying that to everything in my life, like at work or with strangers or friends in a general way. But with my father, yes, that’s where I get stuck, because there are things that don’t make sense to me.

People keep saying the hospital records line up, and the donation emails are all accounted for, and that I’m reading too much into it. But when I actually compare the timestamps, and then I see missing attachments in some of the email chains, and then certain people from the community suddenly get vague or avoid answering very simple questions… I mean, to me, that isn’t nothing. That feels like someone is trying not to say what really happened.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I have the same level of suspicion in every area of my life. It’s concentrated around that. But around that, yes, I do believe something is being hidden.

Do you think your suspiciousness about people hiding things from you is a part of your general way of thinking about people and situations, or is it mostly limited to the circumstances surrounding your father's death?

It’s mostly limited to my father’s death. I know I’ve said that already, but that’s really the center of it. I don’t go into every situation thinking people are hiding things from me. Like at work, if someone sends me a report or says they fixed something, I may check it because that’s part of my job, but I’m not assuming there’s some hidden motive behind it.

But with my father’s death, it’s different. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records line up, and that the donation emails are accounted for, and that I’m connecting things that don’t need to be connected. But when I compare the timestamps, and I see missing attachments, and then certain people from the community avoid my questions or suddenly get vague when I ask something direct, I don’t know how I’m supposed to ignore that. To me, that looks like someone is hiding what really happened.

So no, I wouldn’t call it my general way of thinking about people. I’m not suspicious of everyone all the time. It’s this specific situation, because there are details there that feel too obvious to dismiss.
Do you think you would have been this suspicious of others before your father's death?

No, I don’t think so. Not like this.

Before my father died, I mean, I could be careful about things, sure. I work with systems, so I’m used to checking details and noticing when something doesn’t line up. But I don’t think I was suspicious of people in this way before all of this. It really started in the period after he died, when I was sorting through his records and messages and trying to make sense of everything.

That was about nine months ago now. And at first I thought I was just organizing things, you know, going through emails, documents, dates, that kind of thing. But the more I looked, the more certain details bothered me, and then I started feeling like people weren’t being straight with me.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I would have been this suspicious before. This has really been going on since after his death, over these past nine months or so.
Was your tendency to question people's intentions something that you noticed in yourself before your father passed away?

No, not really. I mean, I’ve always been someone who checks things and asks follow-up questions, especially because of the kind of work I do, but this specific tendency to wonder what people are leaving out or whether their answers are too convenient… that really wasn’t something I noticed in myself before my father passed away.

It started after that, when I was going through his records and messages and trying to organize everything. That was about nine months ago. At first it felt like normal sorting, just trying to understand what happened and keep the paperwork straight, but then I started noticing things that didn’t sit right with me. And once that started, I found myself questioning people’s intentions around that situation much more than I ever had before.
Do you think people would generally try to take advantage of you if they had the chance?

I don’t think so, not generally. I mean, I’m not walking around assuming most people are waiting for some opening to use me or trick me.

There are situations where anyone can be taken advantage of, I guess — like if you’re too trusting with money, or if you don’t read a contract, or if you rely on someone who has their own interest in the outcome. I’m aware of that. But that feels more like common sense than a belief that people in general are out to get me.

If you mean day to day, like coworkers, neighbors, people at a store, no, I don’t usually think, “They’d take advantage of me if they could.” I might be cautious if something seems off, but I don’t automatically assume bad intentions from everyone. It’s more that in certain situations, when the details don’t add up, I start wondering what someone is leaving out. But as a general belief about people? No, I don’t think I’d say that.
Did you consider yourself a trusting person before your father's death?

Yes, I think I probably was more trusting before he died. Not blindly trusting, exactly — I’ve always been the kind of person who checks details and wants things to make sense — but I didn’t used to sit with this feeling that I had to look behind what people were saying.

That really changed after my father died, when I started going through his records and messages. That’s when all of this began, roughly nine months ago. At first it was just practical stuff, sorting documents, trying to understand what needed to be handled, but over time I started feeling less able to just accept things at face value.

So before that, yes, I’d say I was more trusting than I am now.
Do you think your tendency to question people's intentions is something that affects most areas of your life, or is it mainly limited to the situation with your father's death?

It’s mainly limited to the situation with my father’s death, I would say. I don’t feel like it has spread into every part of my life.

I still go to work, I handle my projects, I answer emails, I sit in meetings, I pay my bills, keep my apartment in order — basically I keep my normal routine. At work, for example, I might double-check things because that’s part of being a systems analyst, but I’m not constantly thinking my coworkers are hiding things from me or trying to mislead me.

Where it gets tense is when the subject comes back to my father’s records, or what certain people said happened, or when I ask family members or people in the community about details that don’t make sense to me. That’s when I feel like I have to press more, and that’s when people seem to get uncomfortable or defensive. So, no, I wouldn’t say it affects most areas of my life. It’s mostly centered around that situation.
Did you ever feel this level of suspicion about people's intentions before your father passed away?

No, not really at this level. I mean, I could be cautious before, sure, and if something seemed odd I’d ask questions, but it wasn’t like this.

This really started after my father died — in that period afterward when I was going through his records and messages and trying to piece things together. That’s when I began feeling like people’s explanations weren’t lining up, and I had to look more closely at what they meant or what they weren’t saying.

So if I’m being accurate, it’s been going on for about nine months now. Before that, I don’t remember having this same kind of suspicion about people’s intentions.
Was your tendency to question people's intentions present before your father's death or did it start after that event?

It started after my father died. I mean, I may have questioned things here and there before, like anyone does, but this particular pattern — this feeling that I need to examine what people are really saying or leaving out — that began in the period after his death.

It’s been about nine months now, roughly. It started when I was sorting through his records and messages, trying to make sense of everything. At first I thought I was just being careful and responsible, going through details properly, but over time I noticed I was questioning people’s intentions much more than I ever had before. So no, I wouldn’t say it was really present before that. It came after.

I usually judge it by the situation. If someone has a clear reason to hide something, or if what they’re saying doesn’t match the facts, then yes, I’m going to question it. But if it’s just ordinary day-to-day interactions, I don’t automatically assume dishonesty. That would be exhausting, honestly.
